rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to test whether selectivity improves for the single critical pair. The current elution window leaves ample room below the 10-minute time-penalty threshold.

Test the upper temperature limit to map selectivity changes and seek full resolution without extending the gradient. Monitor all neighboring pairs, since temperature may change elution order and create a new critical pair.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity because warming improves one close pair but causes another to converge. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates this effect, with sufficient time margin to accommodate increased retention.

Use a shallower gradient at the best temperature tested to improve separation of the remaining critical pair and probe slope-dependent selectivity. The current last-peak time of 6.81 minutes provides room to lengthen the gradient without necessarily incurring a time penalty.

Combine the shallower gradient’s increased spacing around peaks 4–5 with a modest temperature increase intended to separate the critical middle pair. This balances the opposing selectivity trends observed at 50 and 60 C while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.
The maximum CRF is achieved; now shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Monitor both close middle pairs, retaining injection 6 as the proven fallback.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to recover the marginal resolution lost in injection 7. This intermediate slope should retain much of the time saving relative to injection 6 while targeting both critical pairs above 1.5.

Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 8’s gradient slope to test a faster elution window. This probes starting-composition effects on the two critical pairs, with injection 8 retained as the faster proven fully resolved method.

Test a faster, warmer gradient to see whether the converging middle pair separates again after an elution-order reversal. This explores a potentially shorter fully resolved regime while retaining injection 8 as the proven fallback.

Raise the starting organic fraction to test whether the reversed critical pair gains separation, while using a shallower slope to protect neighboring pairs. This targets full resolution in the faster high-temperature regime.

Return to the successful 55 C regime and lower the starting organic fraction to improve the pair that limited gradient shortening. A 10-minute gradient tests whether that selectivity gain permits full resolution faster than injection 8.

Slightly flatten injection 12’s gradient to bring its marginal pair above R = 1.5 while checking that the other close pair remains resolved. This could preserve maximum CRF with a last-peak time shorter than injection 8’s.

Test whether a steeper gradient at 50 C can improve the temperature-sensitive close pair while the low starting organic fraction protects its neighbors. This explores a substantially faster regime, retaining injection 13 as the shortest proven fully resolved method.

Test a shallower gradient at 40 C, where the critical middle compounds appear to elute in the opposite order from the 50 C runs. The slope change may therefore improve their separation, revealing an alternative fully resolved regime below the time-penalty threshold.

Explore cooler selectivity with a lower starting organic fraction to separate the middle cluster without extending retention beyond 10 minutes. This tests an alternative resolution window while preserving injection 13 as the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Refine the proven 55 C window with a slope between injections 7 and 8, targeting full resolution with less retention than injection 8. This also tests whether a higher starting organic fraction gives more balanced critical-pair resolution than injection 13.

Test the fast, high-temperature regime with a lower starting organic fraction to protect early and middle-pair spacing. The steeper gradient may separate the reversed critical pair, potentially yielding a substantially shorter fully resolved method.

Test whether lowering temperature restores early-pair resolution at the higher starting organic fraction while improving middle-cluster selectivity. This targets a shorter alternative to injection 13, which remains the fastest proven method with maximum CRF.

Test cooler selectivity in a shifted, moderately shallow gradient window to seek a faster fully resolved alternative. Injection 13 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method; this run checks whether the lower-temperature critical pair benefits enough from the reduced slope.

Shorten the programmed gradient around injection 13 while lowering its endpoint to limit the slope increase. This tests the faster boundary of the proven resolution window; injection 13 remains the fully resolved fallback.

Back off the endpoint by one grid step after injection 21 lost resolution, restoring injection 13’s successful gradient slope with a shorter programmed gradient. Check that the lower final organic fraction still elutes the last compound promptly.

Refine the established 55 C regime by flattening injection 9’s gradient to recover its unresolved pair. The higher starting organic fraction may provide more balanced resolution margins while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Extend injection 23 by one gradient-time step to bring its remaining critical pair above 1.5 while retaining the stronger resolution margin of the other close pair. The last peak is expected near 9 minutes, allowing a potentially more robust maximum-CRF alternative without a time penalty.

Use the final injection to refine the proven 55 C region with a slope between injections 6 and 8, seeking balanced resolution margins while retaining maximum CRF. Injections 13 and 22 remain the fastest demonstrated fully resolved methods, with the last peak at 7.60 minutes.
